stories.headline: Fed Minutes Reveal Unanimous Support for September Rate Hike; More Increases Likely Ahead
stories.summary:
Minutes released Wednesday from the Federal Reserve's most recent policy meeting show that all 19 officials backed the decision to raise interest rates in September, with many supporting the move to guard against the risk of intensifying inflation. The unanimous vote reflects a degree of internal unity at the central bank that is notable given ongoing political and economic pressures.

Most Fed officials signaled that at least one additional rate increase will likely be necessary before the end of the year to bring inflation back toward the central bank's 2% target. Inflation currently runs at 3.4%, outpacing wage growth, while average gasoline prices have risen to $4.37 per gallon and the cost of basic goods including beef remains at record highs.

The Fed's tightening cycle has wide economic implications, affecting mortgage rates, consumer credit, business borrowing costs, and the broader investment climate. Rising borrowing costs have already pushed mortgage applications to their lowest level since February 2025, adding strain to the housing market. The minutes provide the clearest signal yet that the central bank does not view its work as finished despite previous rate increases.

stories.headline: FBI Arrests 18-Year-Old Alleged ISIS Sympathizer in Mall of America Terror Plot
stories.summary:
The FBI on Wednesday announced the arrest of Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, of Minnesota, who investigators say pledged allegiance to ISIS and spent months discussing plans to carry out a mass shooting at the Mall of America in Bloomington. According to federal court documents, Mohamud purchased an AK-47-style rifle, four magazines, and approximately 200 rounds of ammunition from an undercover FBI employee on Tuesday; the rifle had been rendered inoperable by agents, though the ammunition was live.

FBI Director Kash Patel said Mohamud "allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS," and President Trump praised the bureau's handling of the case. Mohamud is charged with knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition while having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and a federal crime of terrorism.

The arrest drew immediate political reaction. Democratic Senate incumbent and Minnesota gubernatorial candidate Amy Klobuchar praised law enforcement and called for "major coordinated investments in anti-terrorism and local law enforcement." Her Republican opponent, Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth, has not yet issued a public statement. The case is being closely watched as a test of domestic counterterrorism procedures and is likely to feature in the upcoming Minnesota gubernatorial campaign.

stories.headline: California Couple Charged With Abusing at Least 14 Surrogate-Born Children
stories.summary:
Los Angeles County prosecutors on Wednesday charged Guojun Xuan, 66, and Silvia Zhang, 39, with multiple counts of child abuse involving at least 14 surrogate-born children, some as young as two months old, as well as dissuading a witness. The pair, who ran their own surrogacy company, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion and pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse.

According to investigators, the couple maintained a home with 21 children — many born through surrogates misled about Zhang's ability to conceive — under the supervision of hired nannies in rooms called "learning centres." Thirty-two motion-activated cameras were allegedly used by the couple to monitor discipline administered by the nannies; footage reportedly shows children being spanked, slapped, and struck. One nanny, Chunmei Li, 58, is accused of striking the two-month-old infant who suffered a head injury days before he was brought to a hospital in May 2025, which triggered the investigation. Li remains at large on a $105,000 warrant.

LA District Attorney Nathan Hochman described the home as a "house of horrors" and said the scale of the alleged abuse was "unprecedented." Twenty-one children were removed from the couple's custody in a July 2025 raid. The couple's attorney maintained that Xuan is innocent and is "being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family." The case has renewed scrutiny of the legal and regulatory framework governing private surrogacy arrangements in the United States.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Launches Massive Missile Barrage on Ukraine, Killing at Least 24 on Putin's Birthday
stories.summary:
Russia launched one of its largest missile attacks of the year against Ukraine overnight, killing at least 24 people and injuring dozens more across multiple cities including Kyiv, Dnipro, Kremenchuk, Zaporizhzhia, and Pryluky in the Chernihiv region. Zelensky said 70 missiles were fired in total, describing the assault as one of Russia's "most vile" attacks and noting that a residential apartment building in Pryluky was destroyed as a birthday "gift" to Vladimir Putin, who turns 74 on Wednesday. Eighteen people, including four children, were killed in that single strike on the five-story building.

Zelensky said Ukraine's air defenses only managed to shoot down "some" of the incoming missiles and renewed appeals to Western allies for additional air defense support packages. Ukrainian forces conducted retaliatory strikes on Russian territory, hitting targets in the Perm, Samara, and Astrakhan regions, including two oil facilities and a military training ground. Zelensky also referenced unspecified activity in the Black Sea, a day after footage showed a large fire engulfing an oil tanker off Sochi.

The attack targeted Ukraine's energy infrastructure, part of an intensified Russian campaign Moscow had signaled in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy facilities. The scale and timing of the strike — on Putin's birthday — drew sharp condemnation from Kyiv and underscored the continued high tempo of the conflict despite earlier diplomatic signals from Western capitals about potential negotiations.

stories.headline: Update: Botched Tennessee Execution Survivor Christa Pike Awake and Speaking; Governor Orders Independent Review
stories.summary:
Convicted murderer Christa Pike has regained consciousness and begun speaking from her hospital bed nearly a week after Tennessee corrections officials failed to execute her via lethal injection, her attorneys announced Wednesday. Pike, 50, survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital administered on September 30 during what prison officials described as a procedure conducted according to protocol. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered an independent review of what went wrong and halted all executions in the state for the remainder of the year.

Defense anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot said Pike did not have a special immunity to the drug but that the pentobarbital most likely spread into tissue beneath the skin rather than entering her bloodstream. "Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot told the BBC. Pike's legal team had warned in advance that her medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting disorder, could cause clots to block the drug from reaching her veins; prison officials used at least seven needles attempting to establish IV lines.

The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended its protocol but has not publicly explained why the execution failed. State protocol does not clearly specify what officials are required to do if an inmate remains alive after a second dose of the drug, according to the Associated Press. The case has reignited national debate over lethal injection procedures and the adequacy of execution protocols, with the mother of Pike's 1995 murder victim describing the failed execution as "a mess."

stories.headline: Sri Lanka's Former First Lady Arrested on Corruption Charges Tied to Children's Hospital Charity
stories.summary:
Sri Lankan anti-corruption authorities arrested former first lady Shiranthi Rajapaksa at her Colombo home on Wednesday, charging her with misusing donations collected for a children's hospital scanner. Rajapaksa, 73, is alleged to have improperly handled 10 million rupees (approximately $30,300) raised by the Siriliya Saviya charity for a specialized scanner at Colombo's Lady Ridgeway Children's Hospital — a scanner that officials say had already been donated by the Chinese government. She had returned Monday from Singapore, where she had been receiving medical treatment, and had sought a court order to prevent her arrest, though the hearing was not scheduled until October 12.

Rajapaksa denied wrongdoing, and a spokesperson for her husband, former President Mahinda Rajapaksa, said the donations remain safely in the charity's accounts and no fraud has occurred. The arrest is the latest in a series of corruption investigations targeting the Rajapaksa family under Sri Lanka's current government led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake. Two of the couple's sons, Namal and Yoshitha Rajapaksa, were arrested earlier this year on separate corruption charges.

Mahinda Rajapaksa served as Sri Lanka's president from 2005 to 2015 and was credited with ending the country's decades-long civil war, but the family's political standing collapsed amid the 2022 economic crisis that triggered widespread protests and ousted his brother Gotabaya from the presidency. The renewed prosecutions signal the current government's intent to pursue long-stalled accountability cases against the country's former ruling dynasty.

stories.headline: Update: Midterm Debates Intensify as Trump Campaigns in Texas With GOP Trailing in Key Races
stories.summary:
With one month until the November midterm elections, a wave of high-profile debates played out Tuesday across competitive Senate and gubernatorial races. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins pointedly distanced herself from President Trump during her debate with Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, calling herself not Trump's 'favorite senator' and opposing both the Iran war and Canadian tariffs. In Georgia, Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms clashed with Republican Rick Jackson in their only scheduled debate of the season.

President Trump traveled to Texas on Wednesday for his third visit in a month, rallying support for Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who trails Democrat James Talarico in what forecasters increasingly view as a competitive race. Trump has been aggressively stumping in traditionally red states as multiple midterm forecasts shift in Democrats' favor, while also floating the possibility of suspending the federal gasoline tax amid voter frustration over fuel costs.

Polls show Republicans struggling on multiple fronts, including healthcare costs, immigration, and the economic fallout from the ongoing Iran conflict. Several Republican senators have privately told reporters that Trump's deportation policies have overreached and are hurting GOP candidates in suburban districts. Democrats, meanwhile, are deploying significant resources into races previously considered safe Republican territory, including Texas gubernatorial and Senate contests.

Republicans have sought to counter by emphasizing crime and public order, while Trump has rolled out financial pledges including $90 payments to Medicare seniors. Analysts from Eurasia Group and other political risk firms have assessed that Republicans are likely to lose the House and potentially the Senate, though the outcome remains contested and Republican strategists argue late momentum is possible.

stories.headline: Update: Tropical Storm Isaias Forms in Gulf of Mexico, Expected to Reach Hurricane Strength Before U.S. Landfall
stories.summary:
Tropical Storm Isaias formed Wednesday in warm waters off eastern Mexico, becoming the first hurricane-strength storm of the Atlantic season as forecasters project it will intensify before striking the U.S. Gulf Coast later this week. As of Wednesday morning, the storm was centered approximately 580 miles southwest of the Mississippi River's mouth, with sustained winds of 40 mph and a northeast trajectory.

The National Hurricane Center projects Isaias could make landfall as a hurricane late Friday or early Saturday, with the most likely impact zone stretching from eastern Louisiana to the western Florida Panhandle. Forecasters warned of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts and urged residents across that corridor to finalize hurricane preparations immediately.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis has declared a state of emergency for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions, activating the state's emergency management plan and authorizing deployment of personnel and equipment. Heavy rainfall is expected across much of the Gulf Coast and southeastern United States through the weekend.

The storm's emergence comes during an unusually quiet Atlantic hurricane season attributed to a strong El Niño pattern that has suppressed storm formation over the Atlantic while driving above-average activity in the Pacific. Isaias represents a significant late-season threat that meteorologists will continue monitoring closely as its track and intensity evolve.

stories.headline: Update: Houthi Rebels Strike Saudi Airports; Tanker Hit in Strait of Hormuz as Yemen Fighting Widens
stories.summary:
Saudi Arabia confirmed Wednesday that three people were injured in Houthi missile and drone attacks on airports in the cities of Najran and Jizan, with both facilities sustaining damage. Houthi Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree announced additional strikes targeting Abha International Airport on Tuesday, though Saudi authorities had not immediately confirmed that attack. The Saudi-led coalition separately said it intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Khamis Mushait, home to a major Saudi military base.

Fighting on the ground in Yemen continued around Dhubab, a strategic coastal town near the Bab al-Mandab Strait whose control has been contested, according to senior Yemeni military officials. Saudi Arabia and its coalition partners have been conducting a campaign to wrest Houthi-controlled territory near the southern Red Sea to secure oil export routes through the region.

Separately, a tanker transiting the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile Monday, the British military reported, with no casualties or environmental damage immediately confirmed. The incident underscores continued maritime risk in the region even as Saudi-backed forces have sought to reduce Houthi influence over key waterways.

The escalation comes as the broader Middle East remains in turmoil, with the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks coinciding with ongoing conflict involving Iran, Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen. The Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian infrastructure mark a significant reignition of fighting that had previously quieted under diplomatic pressure.

stories.headline: Nobel Prize in Chemistry Awarded for Solving Century-Old Mystery of Life's Molecular Asymmetry
stories.summary:
The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded Wednesday to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japan's Kenso Soai for resolving a foundational mystery in biology and chemistry: why living organisms exclusively use one mirror-image form of molecules rather than a 50-50 mixture. The phenomenon, known as chirality, refers to the property of certain molecules that exist in two forms that are mirror images of each other — much like left and right hands — but are not interchangeable.

Kagan, working at Université Paris-Sud, made the initial breakthrough in 1986, discovering a method to manipulate chemical reactions to produce a significant excess of one mirror-image molecule over the other. Soai, of Tokyo University of Science, advanced the work further, publishing a landmark 1995 paper in Nature describing the first chemical reaction capable of producing only the desired version of an organic molecule — a property known as homochirality — and finally achieving controlled homochiral reactions in 2003.

The practical consequences of the discovery are profound, particularly for medicine. Chiral molecules behave differently in the human body depending on their orientation; one version of a drug may be therapeutic while its mirror image is inert or harmful. The most notorious example is Thalidomide, prescribed to pregnant women in the 1950s for morning sickness — its right-handed form was effective, but its left-handed counterpart caused severe birth defects in thousands of children.

Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, called the laureates' chemical reactions 'spectacular,' noting they addressed a mystery more than a century old. The award follows earlier Nobel announcements this week in physics and medicine, completing the scientific Nobel prizes for 2026.

stories.headline: Update: British Police Arrest Seventh Suspect in Iranian-Backed Plot Against U.S. Bomber Base
stories.summary:
British police arrested a 22-year-old on suspicion of terrorism offenses connected to an alleged Iranian-backed plot against RAF Fairford, the British air base from which U.S. B-1 bombers have conducted strikes on Iran. The arrest marks the first made as a result of Britain's formal counterterrorism investigation, distinct from the initial rushed police response that netted five men last Sunday — all subsequently released on bail after no weapons or explosives were found, though they did possess gasoline.

U.S. officials had warned of a possible imminent attack even before the initial arrests, prompting a base lockdown, the evacuation of families, and ultimately the withdrawal of the B-1 bombers back to the United States over the weekend. A senior U.S. official noted the bombers had been parked close enough to the perimeter fence to be vulnerable to a drone attack — a tactic that has proliferated since Ukraine demonstrated its effectiveness in the Russia war.

Vice President J.D. Vance and President Trump both publicly acknowledged Iran's connection to the alleged plot, with Vance warning that those who made the threat 'got themselves a big problem.' Officials say one of the specific threats involved a possible drone strike, consistent with Iranian-backed tactics seen elsewhere. The incident represents a direct extension of the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict into European soil.

stories.headline: ABC, Disney Argue FCC License Review Is Unconstitutional Retaliation; Federal Judge to Rule by Mid-October
stories.summary:
ABC and its parent company Disney faced off against the Trump administration in federal court Tuesday, asking a judge to block the Federal Communications Commission from conducting an accelerated review of ABC's broadcast licenses. ABC attorney Beth Wilkinson argued the process was chilling the network's editorial decisions just weeks before the midterm elections, comparing it to having one's 'head on the guillotine.' The court did not issue an immediate ruling, ordering additional briefings from both sides before a decision expected no earlier than mid-October.

The FCC ordered eight ABC-owned stations to submit license renewal applications years ahead of schedule, a move ABC and Disney say is unconstitutional retaliation for coverage that President Trump dislikes. Trump has repeatedly and publicly criticized ABC, and the lawsuit filed in August names both the FCC and Commissioner Brendan Carr. ABC's attorneys framed the case as a First Amendment threat not just to their network but to press freedom broadly.

The government countered on two fronts: arguing procedurally that the case belongs in a different venue and not before the district court, and substantively that ABC had failed to demonstrate irreparable harm or that its First Amendment rights had been violated. The case is one of several ongoing legal disputes between the Trump administration and news organizations, including the Associated Press, over coverage and White House access since Trump's return to office.

stories.headline: Audio: Ken Paxton Privately Blames Iran War, Gas Prices for Texas Senate Campaign Struggles
stories.summary:
Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton privately told donors and lobbyists at a closed-door Washington fundraiser last month that the Iran war and elevated gas prices were damaging his campaign, according to audio obtained by Axios. 'I don't make the decisions,' Paxton said, in a candid acknowledgment of the headwinds facing Republicans in the 2026 midterm cycle. The recording was confirmed by seven outlets and represents one of the more unguarded assessments by a senior Trump ally of the political environment.

Paxton is running to capture a Texas Senate seat while simultaneously navigating a public divorce from state Sen. Angela Paxton, who has urged voters to support his campaign even as she accuses him of adultery. The Texas race had been seen as a relatively safe Republican hold, but Paxton's private remarks suggest internal anxiety about national conditions overwhelming down-ballot candidates.

The audio is significant as an indicator of how the Iran war — and its downstream effect on energy prices — is fracturing Republican messaging ahead of November. Republicans on the campaign trail have generally defended the administration's foreign policy publicly while privately expressing concern about voter sentiment on economic pain tied to the conflict. Democrats are expected to use elevated gas prices as a central midterm argument.

stories.headline: Third Anniversary of October 7 Hamas Attacks: Kibbutz Survivors Grapple with Rebuilding as Hostage Crisis Lingers
stories.summary:
Three years after the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, communities along Israel's Gaza border are marking the anniversary amid ongoing grief, displacement, and unresolved trauma. At Kibbutz Nir Oz — one of the hardest-hit communities, sitting just over a mile from the Gaza border — roughly one in four residents was either killed or taken hostage. Of the 76 people kidnapped from the kibbutz, all living hostages have been returned, but the physical and psychological reconstruction of the community is far from complete.

The kibbutz remains largely deserted, with fire-damaged homes demolished and reinforced safe rooms left standing as skeletal reminders of the assault. Surviving residents described the difficulty of deciding how to rebuild, with some advocating that damaged structures be preserved as evidence of what occurred. The anniversary also prompted new National Security Council warnings to Jewish communities abroad.

The October 7 attacks, carried out by Hamas's elite Nukhba force along with other Palestinian fighters and civilian participants, killed approximately 1,200 Israelis and resulted in around 250 hostages being taken to Gaza. The assault triggered Israel's ongoing military campaign in Gaza, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and remains a source of deep international division. Supporters of Israel's military response argue it is necessary to eliminate Hamas and secure the release of remaining hostages; critics, including many international human rights organizations, have condemned the scale of civilian casualties and destruction in Gaza.
